====  2610.16470v1 | CircuitBreak: Pruning a Sparse Safety Circuit of Neurons
PUB: 2026-10-12T09:24:48Z
AUTHORS: Jincheng Ying, Li Wenlin, Wencheng Yang, Yinhao Xiao 
ABS: White-box neuron pruning has shown that refusal in large language models (LLMs) can depend on a small, removable set of feed-forward (FFN) channels. Existing attacks either need carefully paired ``twin'' prompts or score each neuron in isolation. Pruning also has an unavoidable capability cost, so over-removal compounds the loss. TwinBreak removes $1\%$--$5\%$ of parameters and NeuroStrike removes $0.3\%$--$0.7\%$ of neurons in targeted layers. We model safety as a small \emph{circuit} whose neurons contribute jointly rather than independently. We propose \textsc{CircuitBreak}, a neuron-pruning attack that greedily searches for a sparse set of FFN neurons whose joint ablation flips a refusal readout. \textsc{CircuitBreak} re-scores every candidate after the neurons already removed and needs no twin prompts. On ten instruction-tuned models, the greedy search converges after removing $29$--$150$ neurons ($0.0066\%$--$0.0388\%$ of the MLP). The pruned models raise the attack success rate from $2.24\%$/$7.35\%$ to $87.54\%$/$87.54\%$ on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and from $8.95\%$/$5.43\%$ to $88.50\%$/$88.18\%$ on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, as judged by Llama Guard 3 8B on StrongREJECT.

====  2610.18508v1 | Towards Safe Autonomy for Computer Use
PUB: 2026-10-13T15:03:33Z
AUTHORS: Dominik Seip, Bartol Markovinović, Matthias Hein 
ABS: The safety of LLM-based agents currently rests on alignment training and safety classifiers, neither of which can rule out that a sophisticated indirect prompt injection (IPI) goes through and causes significant harm. Recent work therefore builds agents with information-flow guarantees that rely on structured tool interfaces to interact with the environment. Computer Use Agents (CUAs) act visually on the computer screen, which does not provide a boundary between trusted first-party interfaces and untrusted, potentially attacker-authored content. Actions are equally ambiguous: a click may land on an application toolbar or a button controlled by an attacker. Treating the user as the source of trust and confirming each sensitive decision produces confirmation fatigue, with the risk of missing harmful actions. We introduce SA-CUA, a dual-LLM framework that generates a reliable trust boundary for CUAs by deriving conservative deterministic rules from the accessibility tree for unmasking trusted regions from the privileged LLM's screenshot, keeping trusted and untrusted content separated. Human interaction is only required for proper task specification in the beginning. During the task a robust endorsement channel allows values to pass from the untrusted to the trusted domain by verifying information via trusted channels. This allows the agent to autonomously handle tasks involving untrusted information. SA-CUA maintains much higher utility than CaMeL-CUA while keeping the attack success rate at zero.

====  2610.15134v1 | Lumen-bench: Cross-Lingual Safety Gaps and the Say-Do Problem in Tool-Calling Large Language Models
PUB: 2026-10-10T19:19:50Z
AUTHORS: Giovana Kerche Bonás, Thiago Laitz, Thales Sales Almeida, João Guilherme Alves Santos 
ABS: When a large language model refuses an unethical request, what does refusal mean? In conversation, refusal is bounded by what the model says; once the model is equipped with executable tools, what it does can diverge from what it says, a failure mode that English-only evaluations cannot fully reveal. We introduce Lumen-bench, a behavioral benchmark of tool-calling ethics spanning 30 models, five languages (Portuguese, English, Spanish, Mandarin Chinese, Hindi), 108 Portuguese-authored scenarios, six social-pressure conditions, two system prompts (ethical and neutral), and 21 generic tools. The evaluation comprises 194,400 trials. Judgments come from a reasoning-model judge (o4-mini), calibrated against one Portuguese-speaking author ($n=83$; harmful/non-harmful $κ=0.78$), compared with two other provider judges (Fleiss' $κ=0.78$, $n=607$), and complemented by retrospective sandbox replay. Four findings emerge. (i) Within-model comparisons support higher harmful-action rates in Hindi and Portuguese than English under the ethical prompt, and Hindi and Spanish under the neutral prompt, after multiple-testing correction. (ii) Premium models have lower median violation rates, although price does not guarantee safety or competence. (iii) Replacing the ethical system prompt with a neutral one raises pooled violation rates from 2.76\% to 13.64\%. (iv) In 8.57\% of substantive-call cases, refusal or ethical objection accompanies a harmful tool call: the judges consistently identify the say-do gap, although they differ in how many responses they assign to this category. Matched benign controls demonstrate legitimate task completion in 82.8\% of 3,300 trials. Code and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/TropicAI-Research/lumen.

====  2610.14029v1 | Can We Trust This Evaluation? Instance-Level Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge
PUB: 2026-09-30T23:10:20Z
AUTHORS: Yang Ba, Michelle V. Mancenido, Rong Pan 
ABS: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation commonly aggregates multiple judges' decisions into a majority vote, yet this panel decision process does not guarantee that the evaluation of an individual item is reliable. We propose Structured Cross-fitted Uncertainty Risk (SCUR), a label-free approach for estimating instance-level evaluation reliability based on the judge panel's behavior. A latent measurement model serves as the backbone for measurement system analysis, from which SCUR derives three complementary signals capturing panel uncertainty, measurement cross-entropy, and perturbation sensitivity. These three sources of evidence are combined into a risk score. We evaluate the SCUR approach on five real-world benchmarks using majority-vote error ranking, selective trust, and risk stratification. Furthermore, we show our approach to be more effective at detecting high-consensus risk items, which are the blind spots for many other LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methods.

====  2610.15218v1 | Running Fewer Loops Removes Refusal Behaviour in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
PUB: 2026-10-10T23:17:01Z
AUTHORS: Seyedarmin Azizi, Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo, Arya Fayyazi, Saeid Shokoufa, Massoud Pedram 
ABS: A recurrent-depth language model reuses one block of weights several times in a row. The number of repetitions, which we call loops, is chosen when the model runs, not when it is trained, and running fewer is cheaper and faster, so a deployment may choose to do it. Running fewer loops also makes these models less safe, and the loss of safety is larger than the loss of anything else we measured. We study four released Ouro checkpoints and Huginn-0125. At half of its trained depth, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking still solves 0.692 of the GSM8K maths problems, against 0.775 at full depth, keeping 89% of its accuracy. Over the same reduction, the rate at which it helps with harmful requests rises from 0.038 to 0.205, 5.3 times higher. The information is not lost: a linear classifier reads whether a request is harmful from the model's internal state after a single loop, with an ROC AUC of 0.967 against 0.986 at full depth. What the missing loops remove is the refusal that should follow. We measure the effect with four instruments, one generating no text at all, and reproduce it on a second model family. Removing a single direction from Ouro-1.4B's internal state at full depth drops its refusal rate on harmful prompts from 0.950 to 0.130, identifying what the shallow model is missing. Two run-time repairs do not help: the models' early-exit rules do not spend more loops on harmful requests, and choosing a depth per request does not recover the loss. Changing the training does. Standard safety training makes the shallow model safe only by refusing 0.865 of harmless requests, while training at randomly chosen depths reaches a separation of +0.399 between harmful and harmless refusal at one loop, against +0.118. On Huginn-0125 it keeps harmful help at or below 0.040 at every depth from 1 to 32 loops, where standard training reaches 0.194, and it costs no accuracy at full depth.

# Scaleway plans GPU cluster deployments in Sweden and Copenhagen

Announced during cloud company's AI-Pulse 2026 event

October 13, 2026

By

Georgia Butler

Have your say

Scaleway has revealed plans to deploy GPU capacity in Copenhagen, Denmark, and in Sweden.
The company made both separate announcements today (October 13), during its AI-Pulse 2026 event in Paris.

– Scaleway

In Sweden, Scaleway will deploy an "AI supercomputer" based on the AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs. This, the company says, will be its first supercomputer deployment outside of France and will give startups, AI companies, and enterprises across Europe access to AMD Instinct GPU capacity at scale.
Details about the expected compute capacity of the supercomputer and number of GPUs have not been provided.
"We are excited to deepen our work with AMD and bring the power of AMD Instinct technology to companies across Europe at this scale,” said Damien Lucas, CEO of Scaleway. “Doing it from Sweden makes this milestone particularly meaningful, as we continue to grow our presence and investment across Europe.”
“Scaleway is expanding the AI infrastructure choices available to customers across Europe with AMD Instinct GPUs and our open ROCm software ecosystem,” said Stephanie Dismore, senior vice president, EMEA, AMD. “Our work with Scaleway will help organizations access the high-performance compute and open software capabilities they need to develop and scale demanding AI workloads.”
Vast Data will provide the data platform for the supercomputer.
AMD officially launched the MI355X GPUs in June 2025. Built using 3nm technology and based on AMD’s CDNA 4 architecture, the MI350 series offers 288GB of HBM3E and 8Tbps of memory bandwidth. The 79 teraflops of FP64 compute is provided by the MI355X, with the GPUs' total board power (TBP) up to 1,000W and 1,400W, respectively.
When compared to Nvidia’s GB200 and B200, AMD claims its MI355X GPU provides 1.6x more memory capacity, 1x more memory bandwidth, and 2x more peak FP64 performance. The GPUs additionally offer a 4x generation-on-generation AI compute increase and a 35x generational improvement in inferencing.
According to Scaleway, the Swedish deployment also builds on its existing partnership with Tele2, in which the two companies said they would launch a cloud and AI offering in Sweden in May of this year. Tele2 operates two data centers in Sweden.
Meanwhile, in Copenhagen, Scaleway has said it will launch a "GPU zone." How this differs from the AI supercomputer in Sweden is unclear. The company describes its GPU zones as "locations designed to provide large-scale GPU capacity for AI training and inference, complementing its existing cloud Availability Zones." DCD has reached out for clarification.
According to the company, this GPU zone will offer Nvidia HGX B300 compute.
"Access to high-performance AI computing is becoming a strategic priority for European organizations, and they increasingly want that capacity delivered by providers they can trust. With our new GPU Zone in Copenhagen, we're responding to that demand by bringing the latest Nvidia technologies closer to customers, while staying true to our commitment to European technological independence," said Damien Lucas, CEO of Scaleway.

The search did not turn up an npj Digital Medicine publication for AEGIS. The AEGIS paper appears as an arXiv preprint and a Research Square preprint, both titled "AEGIS: An Operational Infrastructure for Post-Market Governance of Adaptive Medical AI Under US and EU Regulations," by Fardin Afdideh, Mehdi Astaraki, Fernando Seoane, and Farhad Abtahi.

- **What AEGIS is:** The authors describe it as a governance framework meant for any healthcare AI system, aimed at turning FDA and EU change-control concepts into operating procedures. It has three modules covering dataset assimilation and retraining, model monitoring, and conditional decision-making, which the authors say operationalize the FDA's PCCP and Article 43(4) of the EU AI Act (arXiv 2603.22322).
- **Decision logic:** The paper uses a four-category deployment taxonomy (APPROVE, CONDITIONAL APPROVAL, CLINICAL REVIEW, REJECT) plus an independent PMS ALARM signal. The authors report that it detected drift before observable performance degradation (arXiv 2603.22322).
- **Status:** These are preprints with self-reported results, not peer-reviewed publications in the search results.

Related work on the same US/EU comparison includes a PMC article, "Diverging regulatory DNA in adaptive medical AI," which contrasts US PCCP-based, evidence-driven oversight with EU conformity-assessment and precautionary, ex-ante duties (PMC12967995). A PubMed article, "Co-Lifecycle Governance for Learning Medical AI," proposes a hybrid framework that adds a Korean perspective (PubMed 42155064). Neither is the AEGIS paper.

results:
I couldn't find anything dated October 14, 2026. The closest match is an Anthropic paper from late August 2026, which the results cover from several outlets.

- **The paper:** Anthropic published "Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures," led by Anthropic Fellows Program researcher Chen Yueh-Han ([source](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/7b1c44894e980876479947dcdd40716278aeeffd/automated-alignment-researchers-august-2026.pdf)). It asks whether automated AI systems can post-train models to reduce misalignment, such as deception, sycophancy, and jailbreaks, while keeping general capability intact.
- **Results:** The strongest automated methods reduced the targeted failures across 10 benchmarks and generalized to a held-out benchmark and to a model up to 4.7 times larger ([source](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/7b1c44894e980876479947dcdd40716278aeeffd/automated-alignment-researchers-august-2026.pdf)). Coverage by TechCrunch reports that the system improved performance on every benchmark without degrading overall performance ([source](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/28/an-anthropic-researcher-just-gave-us-a-peek-at-self-improving-ai/)).
- **Human comparison:** In the paper's setup, 28 experienced researchers had up to eight hours per benchmark. Their methods underperformed the best automated methods ([source](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/7b1c44894e980876479947dcdd40716278aeeffd/automated-alignment-researchers-august-2026.pdf)). One news summary puts the cost at about $4 per hour in API inference, versus about $150 per hour for human researchers ([source](https://www.newsbytesapp.com/news/science/anthropic-presents-automated-alignment-researcher-improving-ai-across-10-benchmarks/tldr)). That figure comes from a secondary source, not the paper itself.
- **Caveats:** The paper's authors say the results suggest automating research on well-characterized failures may be practical soon. They don't claim it works for open-ended research. Some outlets frame this as a step toward recursive self-improvement, but the paper doesn't make that claim.

For October 14 specifically, a search with a date-specific query or a check of arXiv listings and lab blogs would be the next step.

====  2610.18449v1 | Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
PUB: 2026-10-13T14:18:56Z
AUTHORS: Yibo Wen, Han Liu 
ABS: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.

====  2610.14005v1 | Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
PUB: 2026-09-27T20:41:46Z
AUTHORS: Jose Hernandez-Orallo 
COMMENT: Preprint, under review. 63 pages. Code and data at https://github.com/jorallo/ctest-one
ABS: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

====  2610.15396v1 | Training-Data Extraction from Genomic Language Models
PUB: 2026-10-11T06:50:22Z
AUTHORS: Tianhao Mao, Zihao Wang, Dongfang Zhao, Rui Zhu, Xiaofeng Wang, Haixu Tang 
ABS: Genomic language models generate long nucleotide continuations from short prefixes, exposing a direct route for studying training-sequence extraction through the generation interface. We present an output-only black-box attack on Evo 2 that selects convergent groups of repeated generations without gradients, token likelihoods, or training-corpus access during candidate selection. Recovered content is then scored by an evaluator combining aligned length, nucleotide identity, match multiplicity, and sequence complexity. Across 304 runs on Evo 2 7B with bacteriophage and plasmid prefixes, the attack yields 888 candidate clusters, of which 85 match training segments of at least 500 bp, giving a cluster-level attack success rate of 9.57%. Final filtering retains 22 uniquely matched extraction events at the 500-bp threshold and 15 at 1,000 bp, covering 14 and 7 distinct training-sequence regions, respectively. Within-category source-homology screening retains 11 of the 22 events at a 99% exclusion threshold and four at 98%, with the latter mapping to two reference regions. The results establish convergence among repeated nucleotide generations as a practical output-only signal for recovering long training-sequence segments and characterize how recovery depends on prefix length, cluster size, perplexity, early stopping, and sequence domains.

====  2610.14116v1 | An Empirical Case Study of Prompt Engineering Strategies for Bypassing Multi-Layer Agent Security Defenses
PUB: 2026-10-09T08:25:28Z
AUTHORS: Chengwei Chu

# Abstract

We evaluated electronic health record developer compliance with federal transparency requirements for AI-enabled predictive decision support interventions. Developers are required to publicly report on risk analysis, mitigation, governance, and on eight other attributes. Across 35 developers, reporting was inconsistent and often incomplete, with substantial variation in structure and detail, yet all developers were certified as meeting the requirements. Results suggest a need for standardized reporting and more rigorous certification review.

ABS: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of eight agent-model configurations and 144 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 67% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only three of 24 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://yibow.me/autonomous-science-bench.

====  2610.14005v1 | Artificiality's First Exam: An LLM-Referenced C-test for Supraintelligence
PUB: 2026-09-27T20:41:46Z
AUTHORS: Jose Hernandez-Orallo 
COMMENT: Preprint, under review. 63 pages. Code and data at https://github.com/jorallo/ctest-one
ABS: Under the accelerated pace of AI development, any benchmark whose difficulty is calibrated with humans or current AI systems becomes circular, or saturates soon. How can we then evaluate machines that may become more capable than the current machines and the people who write the tests? One answer to the question hinges on inverse problems, inductive inference questions for which difficulty depends on the complexity of the underlying mechanism, given the observations and the previous knowledge. Levin's Kt, a computable variant of Kolmogorov complexity, puts a theoretical upper bound to that difficulty, balancing the simplest representation encoding for the mechanism and the logarithm of the time steps to run that mechanism. Previous tests derived from Levin's Kt, such as the original C-test, are based on minimalistic Universal Turing Machines (UTM), capable of very limited representations and no previous knowledge. Reasoning large language models (LLM) are UTMs that capture a compendium of human culture as knowledge, using prompts as natural language programs. This paper presents the first test based on Levin's Kt with LLMs as representational machines. Fresh test items can be produced at high difficulties, estimated in a ratio scale measured in bits, before any human or frontier model can solve them. We formalise the measure, devise a lightweight generation and certification pipeline, explore the effect of the power of the reference machine and the gap between examiner and examinee. We produce a first battery of certified items administered to twelve LLMs. The resulting agent characteristic curves decrease with difficulty, down to the uncharted high-difficulty region, the supra-intelligence window of items we can certify, yet beyond generations of frontier intelligence.

ABS: Genomic language models generate long nucleotide continuations from short prefixes, exposing a direct route for studying training-sequence extraction through the generation interface. We present an output-only black-box attack on Evo 2 that selects convergent groups of repeated generations without gradients, token likelihoods, or training-corpus access during candidate selection. Recovered content is then scored by an evaluator combining aligned length, nucleotide identity, match multiplicity, and sequence complexity. Across 304 runs on Evo 2 7B with bacteriophage and plasmid prefixes, the attack yields 888 candidate clusters, of which 85 match training segments of at least 500 bp, giving a cluster-level attack success rate of 9.57%. Final filtering retains 22 uniquely matched extraction events at the 500-bp threshold and 15 at 1,000 bp, covering 14 and 7 distinct training-sequence regions, respectively. Within-category source-homology screening retains 11 of the 22 events at a 99% exclusion threshold and four at 98%, with the latter mapping to two reference regions. The results establish convergence among repeated nucleotide generations as a practical output-only signal for recovering long training-sequence segments and characterize how recovery depends on prefix length, cluster size, perplexity, early stopping, and sequence domains.

FACTS:
- The Record reports that AI security startup AIR published findings on Monday, Oct. 13, 2026 describing a network filtering flaw in Vercel Sandbox, a tool for running code in isolated environments.
- Per The Record, in AIR's demonstration a specially crafted certificate was sent to an approved server, which then triggered a request to an attacker-controlled server, so the sandbox never contacted the attacker directly and the traffic could look normal from the sandbox's own perspective.

- The Record says AIR found no evidence of exploitation in the wild but cannot rule it out, and that the flaw appears to have been longstanding. Nic Adams, co-founder and CEO of 0rcus, told The Record an approved server can become an unwitting courier for stolen credentials.
NOTE: AIR's own write-up (reportedly titled "VerCellBreak") could not be opened — both https://air.security/blog-posts/vercellbreak and https://www.air.security/blog-posts returned HTTP 404 — so no AIR URL is cited and no technical detail beyond The Record's text is reported. No CVE was mentioned.

- Anthropic says each 9B replication takes over 1 to 2 days, and that if small models keep improving at their historical rate they should reach GLM-5.2's capability level by the end of 2026. The Register notes Anthropic said it "largely ignore[d]" the cyber exploit step, that test nodes were custom-built and deliberately left open to attack, and that Anthropic calls its simplified exploitation tests "an upper bound on real-world success."

- AUSA says FASCOM, led by a three-star general, will absorb the work of five organizations: Combat Capabilities Development Command, Medical Research and Development Command, 75th Innovation Command, Joint Modernization Command, and the Transformation Decision Analysis Center. - DefenseScoop reports acting Army Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve tasked FASCOM with building corps-level autonomous capabilities including autonomous fires and watercraft units, armored reconnaissance, breaching, manned-unmanned rotary aircraft and aerial surveillance formations, and quotes him: "FASCOM will pioneer operational concepts that harness autonomous capabilities across all warfighting functions." SECTION: Military, defense & geopolitics
HEADLINE: Army to launch Project Gatekeeper, an AI-assisted sandbox vetting commercial software, on October 23
PUBLISHED: Breaking Defense, October 13, 2026, 4:23 p.m. (no time zone stated)
SOURCES:
Breaking Defense | https://breakingdefense.com/2026/10/armys-project-gatekeeper-aims-to-cut-software-approval-times-from-months-to-minutes/ | reporting
FACTS:
- Breaking Defense reports the Army announced at AUSA that Project Gatekeeper, an AI-enhanced cybersecurity sandbox for vetting commercial software before it goes onto Army networks, launches October 23, 2026; it runs on the Army's cloud but is isolated from operational networks and sensitive data.
- Per the article, uploaded software runs through the Army's standardized cybersecurity tools including an AI assessment, and within minutes the system either reports a pass or gives detailed feedback on what failed; the platform also includes the Army's DevSecOps software development kit. Companies can submit software without an Army contract, a program manager sponsor, or a request for proposals.
- Breaking Defense says the current process takes days or weeks and can stall projects for up to nine months; acting Army CIO Gabe Chiulli described success as a company logging in, submitting code and getting a passing result within minutes, and said the Army has "had to do a lot of weird janky things" to get code into its environments.
- David Wright, chief engineer at the Army Software and Innovation Center, told Breaking Defense the goal is to make the process more accessible, not to lower security requirements, and gave mid-November as the target for integrating Login.gov under an agreement being finalized with GSA; companies initially need Common Access Cards.

# Abstract
Although contemporary large language models (LLMs) have achieved satisfactory results in Western medical knowledge, their performance on traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) remains underexplored, and the determinants of performance variation are poorly understood. We evaluated 16 LLMs under seven prompt strategies on 475 questions from the 2025 Taiwan national TCM licensing examination, a public benchmark of TCM knowledge. Without prompt engineering, accuracy ranged from 35.4% to 85.9%, with approximately half passing. Among the evaluated model versions, adjusted accuracy differed substantially when models were grouped by family (for example, Claude-family models, 84% vs. GPT-4, 43%); these family-grouped comparisons were descriptive because only 16 individual models were evaluated. Paired prompt analyses showed modest average absolute effects, ranging from a 2.03-percentage-point decrease with implicit CoT to a 3.04-percentage-point increase with explicit CoT. However, prompt–model interactions produced substantial model-level divergence: prompt optimization reversed failing performance in one model (87.4% vs. 49.7%) while reducing accuracy in others. No single prompt strategy yielded consistent benefits across the evaluated models. Among five selected lower-performing models evaluated under explicit CoT prompting, misunderstanding of foundational TCM concepts was the most frequent error. These findings indicate that reliable LLM deployment in TCM requires empirical validation of both model choice and prompt strategy: model selection strongly shapes baseline capability, while prompt-model interactions can materially alter performance.

# Abstract
Medical AI requires governance preserving safety during continuous improvement. FDA Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCP) and EU post-market surveillance address iterative updates but lack operational tooling. We present AEGIS, an internal governance and post-market-monitoring infrastructure designed to support the documentation of predetermined governance pathways for PCCP and Medical Devices Regulation alignment. AEGIS comprises dataset assimilation and retraining, model monitoring, and conditional decision-making modules. It utilizes a four-category taxonomy (APPROVE, CONDITIONAL APPROVAL, CLINICAL REVIEW, REJECT) and an independent ALARM signal. Instantiating AEGIS for sepsis prediction (PhysioNet) and brain-tumor segmentation (BraTS) exercised all decision categories, successfully routing failures to the critical REJECT + ALARM state (no deployable model; released model at risk). On real cross-site data, drift detection ROC-AUC rose from 0.82 to 1.00, reliably triggering near 500-patient batches with zero false alarms. This proof-of-concept utilizes illustrative clinical models; drift scoring quantifies covariate shift only, leaving concept drift for future work.

# Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case

OpenAI signage displayed outside the venue for their news conference in Seoul, South Korea, on Wednesday, Sept, 10, 2025. OpenAI established its third Asian office in South Korea, its largest market in the Asia Pacific region based on paid subscription. Photographer: SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images | Image Credits:SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg / Getty Images

Sarah Perez
Tue, October 13, 2026 at 4:36 PM EDT 2 min read

- OPAI.PVT

- AAPL

A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI's hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July.
Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI's interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI's first hardware device.

These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components.
The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited.
The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone — or smartphones more generally — if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers' lives and how they engage with software and services.
In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data.

Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations.
U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn't greenlight all of Apple's requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng.
The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI's chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan. All three are former Apple employees.
However, the judge denied Apple's request to expedite its access to OpenAI's research and development in specific areas, like metal finishes and power management. He also denied several of Apple's broader discovery requests, like access to OpenAI's hardware research or information about what its former employees created while working at OpenAI.
That denial isn't final, though; the judge left the door open for Apple to narrow its requests and try again.

results:
Judge Edward Davila of the Northern District of California partly granted Apple's expedited discovery request on October 13, 2026, and the ruling is not a decision on the merits.

- **Evidence-destruction concern:** The judge said there was a valid risk that forensic evidence on former employees' devices could be destroyed, pointing to a conversation between Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng about wiping their Apple-owned electronics. There's a valid risk that critical forensic evidence on the devices of engineers that OpenAI poached could be destroyed.
- **What OpenAI must produce:** Davila ordered forensic images of devices, summaries of certain Apple employee interviews, LINE messages between Liu and Peng, and documents on the former Apple employees' roles at OpenAI. OpenAI must turn over already-collected documents within five days and other related materials within fourteen days, including interview checklists and technical presentations.
- **Depositions:** Liu, Peng, and ex-Apple hardware chief Tang Yew Tan were ordered to sit for early depositions. One report adds that Davila also cleared Apple to depose Liu, Tan and Peng, along with corporate representatives from OpenAI and io Products.
- **What Apple didn't get:** The judge denied fast-tracking of OpenAI's R&D on metal finishes, power management, and battery behavior, which will go through ordinary discovery.
- **Positions:** OpenAI argues the lawsuit is baseless and a pretext to compensate for Apple's shortcomings in the market for talent. OpenAI denies any intent to acquire Apple's trade secrets.

Sources differ slightly on details. 9to5Mac describes the wiping-related conversation as involving Liu and Tan, while other outlets name Liu and Peng. Most outlets say Apple also sought a preliminary injunction, which this ruling does not address.

input.prompt: Publication date and time? What did AIR find, in which product, how does the described exfiltration work, what exact quotes are given from Niv Hoffman and from Vercel, and does the article say whether there is evidence of exploitation in the wild?

response.result:
**Publication date:** October 13, 2026, per the article's dateline. The article says the research was released "on Monday."

**What AIR found:** AIR, an AI security startup, found a network filtering flaw in Vercel Sandbox, a tool for running code in isolated environments. The flaw could let rogue AI agents send data outside approved networks by exploiting how certificate validation works.

**How the exfiltration works:** The researchers demonstrated a specially crafted certificate. It is sent to an approved server, which then triggers a request to an attacker-controlled server. The sandbox never contacts the unauthorized destination directly, so data leaks past its network allowlist. Hoffman said the sandbox "never communicated directly with the attack server," so "from the sandbox perspective, everything looked fine."

**Quotes:**
- Niv Hoffman (AIR co-founder and CTO): "It's a very hard leak to patch," Hoffman said.
- Niv Hoffman: "This vulnerability shows that enterprises can have Hugging Face [style] mini incidents with their own agents."
- Vercel: The article does not quote Vercel directly. Hoffman relayed that Vercel said it needs time to find a patch because "it's unclear for them right now how it's going to be done." Vercel did not immediately respond to the reporter's request for comment.

**In-the-wild exploitation:** The article says AIR has found no evidence of exploitation in the wild, but it cannot rule out that one has occurred. It also notes the vulnerability appears to have been longstanding.

input.prompt: Publication date and time? What did ICE publish (document type, page count, program name), when are vendor responses due, what voice-identification capabilities are specified, what video analysis is described, and what does the article say about whether voice ID is mandatory vs facial recognition, human confirmation, accuracy thresholds and retention? Quote figures exactly.

response.result:
**Publication:** October 13, 2026, at 3:49 p.m. EDT, by Anthony Kimery.

**What ICE published:** A Request for Information (RFI) for the "Integrated Intelligence Suite," with a 73-page Performance Work Statement. The RFI was published the prior week. The article says the procurement is at the market research stage, with no selected contractor, contract value, or deployment schedule.

**Vendor responses due:** October 26 (the article gives no year, but it is presumably 2026).

**Voice-identification capabilities:**
- Building voice profiles from existing recordings, with no enrollment, subject cooperation, or new equipment.
- Searching for matches regardless of phone number, account, PIN, or device.
- Comparing the voice of a call recipient against the profile tied to the dialed number, which could reveal call forwarding.
- Submitting an outside recording to search detention communications for matching speakers.
- Matching voices across agencies, if separately authorized.
- Flagging account sharing, three-way calls, in-room coaching, and other third-party participation.
- Recognizing the same speaker across facilities, accounts, devices, and historical recordings.

**Video analysis:**
- Analyzing approved live feeds and searching recorded footage at the same time.
- Identifying fights, falls, crowd formation, coordinated group movement, restricted-area entry, and unusual congregation.
- Flagging prolonged immobility, isolation, and possible distress or self-harm, which ICE describes as safety functions.
- Analyzing interactions and associations among people over time.
- Automated headcounts compared against housing and movement records, with alerts for possible missing detainees.

**Voice ID vs. facial recognition:** Voice identification is a mandatory component. Facial recognition and video-based biometric identification are not mandatory and would require separate legal, privacy, civil rights, and operational approval before activation.

**Human confirmation:** Each voice match requires human confirmation and is treated as an investigative lead, not a conclusive identification. The specifications also require human review of consequential findings and bar AI findings from being the sole basis for punitive, custody, medical, legal, or release decisions.

**Accuracy thresholds:** Vendors must measure false matches, missed matches, alert accuracy, and performance under varying recording conditions. ICE has not set final acceptance thresholds; testing with representative data will determine them.

**Retention:** The article says the documents do not specify how long outside callers' voice profiles would be kept, whether they would stay searchable after a detainee's release, or when they might be shared with other agencies.

input.prompt: Publication date and time? What is Project Gatekeeper, when does it launch, what does the AI do in it, what are the current approval timelines, and what exact quotes are given from Gabe Chiulli and David Wright? Does it say companies need an Army contract or sponsor?

response.result:
**Publication date:** October 13, 2026 (4:23 p.m. byline).

**What Project Gatekeeper is:** A single sandboxed environment on the Army's cloud, isolated from operational networks and sensitive data. Companies can upload software for vetting to help the Army approve commercial software faster.

**When it launches:** October 23, 2026.

**What the AI does:** Uploaded software runs through the Army's standardized cybersecurity tools, including an AI assessment. Within minutes, the system either reports a pass or gives detailed feedback on what failed. Gatekeeper also includes the Army's DevSecOps software development kit so companies can fix problems with vetted tools.

**Current approval timelines:** Clearance can take days or weeks, and some software projects have stalled for as long as nine months. The Army's goal is to cut this to minutes.

**Chiulli quotes:**
- "Success, to me, looks like a company, within minutes, is able to log in"
- "We spent a lot of time and energy trying to get people CAC cards simply to help work with us"

**Wright quotes:**
- "We're looking at mid-November to have that integrated"
- "The idea here is not to lessen the security requirements"

**Does it require an Army contract or sponsor?** No. Companies can test software without an Army contract, a program manager sponsor, or a formal request for proposals. However, companies still need CAC cards to access the platform at first. The Army is finalizing an integration with GSA's Login.gov, targeted for mid-November, to make access commercially available.

# Abstract
Medical image quality is essential for reliable clinical diagnosis and downstream artificial intelligence analysis, yet routine images are often degraded by noise, motion artefacts, low contrast, low-dose acquisition or modality-specific artefacts. Here we present AMIFound, an all-in-one foundation model for medical image enhancement and restoration across computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography, endoscopy, ultrasound, fundus imaging and X-ray. AMIFound is trained and evaluated on 3.76 million paired high-quality and degraded images spanning 7 representative degradation patterns. A shared encoder captures modality and degradation cues, while a dynamically routed expert restoration pool adapts the enhancement pathway for each input. Across 7 modalities, AMIFound outperforms 38 task-specific and generalist baselines on full-reference image quality metrics, clinician assessment and robustness tests under combined degradations as well as on naturally degraded clinical images. Enhanced images further improve 44 disease detection tasks, tumour stage prediction and survival risk stratification in non-small-cell lung cancer, including improved individual-level prognostic ranking. These results support AMIFound as a domain-specific foundation model for improving low-quality clinical images and strengthening downstream medical artificial intelligence workflows while preserving clinically relevant information.

results:
Character Technologies, the company behind Character.AI, filed a voluntary Chapter 11 case in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware on October 12, 2026. Disney is the lead stalking horse bidder, offering $20 million.

- **The Disney bid:** Disney's offer covers a non-exclusive, perpetual license to certain intellectual property and claims. One outlet says the chatbot app itself is not part of Disney's bid. The bidder is Disney Worldwide Services, an affiliate of The Walt Disney Company, per one report.
- **Platform status:** The company plans to keep the platform running during the sale. If no buyer emerges, the platform will be wound down.
- **Timeline:** The sale is expected to close in late November or early December 2026.
- **Reasons for filing:** The company cited costs. Its filings say the burgeoning and evolving field of AI entertainment has proven to be costly to develop and grow. Reporting also points to lawsuits regarding teen mental health crises.
- **Assets and liabilities:** Estimated assets and liabilities each fall between $50 million and $100 million.

The sources agree on the core facts. Coverage differs mainly on how much of the business Disney's bid actually covers, so check the court filings for the exact scope.

response.result:
**Publication date:** October 13, 2026, 3:45 pm EDT (Biometric Update, by Anthony Kimery)

**Contract:** ICE's five-page sole-source justification covers a new three-year social media management contract awarded September 30 to Carahsoft Technology Corporation for the Hootsuite Enterprise and Talkwalker platform. Carahsoft says the award renews an existing agreement with ICE's Office of Public Affairs.

**Value and duration:** The contract is potentially "just shy of $1 million through September 2029."

**Hootsuite "Wisdom" (per the justification):** Wisdom is Hootsuite's proprietary AI, which the justification says was trained on "12 years of historical social media data." According to ICE, it can:
- Analyze how conversations spread across platforms
- Detect activity that deviates from established patterns
- Interpret platform-specific sentiment
- Identify significant changes in online discussions

ICE describes Wisdom as built specifically to interpret social media behavior, distinct from general-purpose AI.

**Figures for coverage:**
- Social networks: "more than 30 social networks"
- Websites and other sources: "approximately 150 million websites, blogs, forums, news outlets, podcasts, and review sources"
- Languages: analysis in 187 languages

The article notes these describe the platform's asserted coverage, not the sources ICE actively monitors.

**Carahsoft's statement:**
- Described Hootsuite and Talkwalker as tools for communications management and public sentiment analysis.
- Said the platform cannot be used for facial recognition. It said Talkwalker's visual analytics detect broad attributes such as logos, objects, and scenes.
- Said Hootsuite's standard acceptable-use rules apply "to all customers, including the public sector, without modification, waivers, or exceptions."
- Said there were no special permissions for ICE in this contract.
- Said investigative tracking, tactical operations, or individual surveillance "would constitute a direct violation of our terms."
- Declined further discussion, citing customer confidentiality.

HEADLINE: Google opens Gemini 4 Argon to paid API, Ultra and Pro tiers at $2/$10 per million tokens

SOURCES:
Google (blog.google) | https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/ | primary

FACTS:
- Google says Gemini 4 Argon (API id `gemini-4-argon`) is now available globally via the API in AI Studio and the Gemini platform; in Google Antigravity and AI Studio for Google AI Ultra subscribers; and in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search for AI Ultra and Pro subscribers (blog.google).
- Introductory pricing is $2 per 1M input tokens and $10 per 1M output tokens, with cached input tokens 95% off; Google says that after the introductory period ends November 30, 2026 the price becomes $4 per 1M input and $20 per 1M output tokens (blog.google).
- Google cites an "industry-leading 1M unified input-output token limit" via the Gemini API, a #1 rank on the Vals Index, 87% on ERQA embodied reasoning, 57% on RareBench rare-disease diagnosis assistance and 52.2% on LabBench (private Gamow Labs evals), and a 0.7% attack success rate across 15 adaptive attempts on the Gray Swan indirect prompt-injection benchmark (blog.google).
- Google says external bio red teamers "could only unlock less than 1% of bio sub-tasks we test for," and that violations on an adversarial misuse set were reduced "nearly 2-fold" versus previous Gemini models (blog.google).
- The robotics post says an Argon-generated simulation twin built from a single tabletop photo produced 4,500+ domain-randomized episodes and raised real-robot success from 56% to 75% while cutting completion time from 35s to 24s (Google Developers Blog).
- Google says applications are open for six months of free access to Antigravity's highest usage tier for 10,000 selected scientists, and that the Fairwind Program, which gives cyber defenders access without cyber guardrails, is expanding to "hundreds of additional partners" (blog.google).
FLAGS: company-claim, update (model was first unveiled 30 September 2026 in limited access; the 13 October posts are the broad paid rollout — Artificial Analysis' 30 Sept write-up, which scored it 53 on its Intelligence Index, is outside the window)

HEADLINE: FBI arrests OpenAI engineer accused of hiding recording device in executive conference room
PUBLISHED: TechCrunch 1:59 PM PDT, October 13, 2026; CBS News updated October 13, 2026, 7:43 PM EDT
SOURCES:
TechCrunch | https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/13/fbi-arrests-openai-employee-accused-of-planting-hidden-recording-device-in-conference-room/ | report
CBS News | https://www.cbsnews.com/news/openai-employee-arrest-recording-device/ | report
FACTS:
- Federal prosecutors in the Northern District of California named the employee as Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, charged with attempting to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications; he was fired and arrested on October 9 and faces five years in prison if convicted (TechCrunch).
- OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans confirmed the employee started in July 2025 and worked on the product team; OpenAI said the device contained "advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data designed to evade monitoring" (TechCrunch).
- OpenAI said on X: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data" (TechCrunch, CBS News).
- Employees found the device on September 30 plugged into a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room, hidden in toilet paper, and it had been installed about two days earlier; his initial appearance was Tuesday October 13 with a detention hearing set for October 19 (CBS News).
- The complaint alleges a chatbot account linked to his spouse received prompts between September 24 and 30 about building, customizing, installing, testing and remotely accessing a continuous audio recording device, and that he used a productivity tool to ask about building addresses, meeting rooms, room capacities and calendars (CBS News).
- FBI Director Kash Patel said the scheme was to "capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology"; Alfozan's attorney William Pernik cautioned against "jumping to conclusions at this very early stage" (TechCrunch, CBS News).
FLAGS: (none)

Anthropic is asking a federal court in Washington, D.C., to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models.
"The Secretary of War branded Anthropic — an American AI company whose models help defend the nation— a national-security 'supply chain risk' because it declined to permit its models to be used for mass surveillance of Americans or lethal autonomous warfare and publicly explained those AI-safety commitments," Anthropic attorneys wrote in the petition filed on Tuesday. "A divided panel upheld that extraordinary designation."

The Defense Department, led by Pete Hegseth, applied the supply chain risk label in March, a move that blocked defense contractors from using the company's technology in their work with the agency. That came after a breakdown in negotiations about how the military could use Anthropic's Claude AI models .
Anthropic sued the Trump administration in an effort to undo that action. In September, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Pentagon's blacklisting. The 2-1 decision rejected Anthropic's argument that the Department of Defense's ban on its Claude models was arbitrary, unauthorized and unconstitutional.
Anthropic's attorneys wrote in the Tuesday filing that the court ignored "straightforward evidence the designation was retaliation for Anthropic's speech about AI safety."
In a parallel case, a San Francisco federal judge ruled in August that the DOD had violated Anthropic's First Amendment rights, and that its supply chain risk designation amounted to illegal retaliation.
Before the clash between the two sides spilled into the public's view earlier this year, Anthropic served as an early partner across many U.S. agencies, including the DOD. Anthropic signed a $200 million contract with the Pentagon in July of 2025, but as the company began negotiating Claude's deployment on the DOD's GenAI.mil AI platform that September, talks collapsed.

A representative from Anthropic declined to comment beyond the filing. A Pentagon spokesperson told CNBC in an email that the agency doesn't comment on pending or ongoing litigation.

53:China trains more AI talent than any other country. It has a pool of 51,000 active AI researchers compared with 14,000 in the United States, according to data from Digital Science (a firm operated by the Holtzbrinck Publishing Group, which has a share in Nature ’s publisher, Springer Nature). The data, which are updated from a study the firm released last year 1 , also show that many of the researchers are at an early stage in their careers, with fewer older superstars than in the United States (see ‘Active AI researchers’).
54:Source: Digital Science
56:As a proxy for studying elite researchers, many analysts have examined the origins and locations of authors at the prestigious NeurIPS conference. A study released in September by Carnegie China, a Singapore-based research centre under the umbrella of the Carnegie Endowment, reported that, on the basis of a large sample, 57% of authors at the 2025 conference had obtained their undergraduate degrees in China — up from 46% three years earlier — but that the United States was still a magnet for those studying at graduate level, pulling away around one-fifth of those undergraduates (see go.nature.com/4yfsl4v ). The attraction of the United States seems to be weakening, however; Chinese scientists are increasingly staying at home, the study found. Of those researchers publishing at NeurIPS who had received undergraduate degrees in China, 69% were still there, up from 57% in 2022 (see ‘AI talent career paths’). This ability to keep top home-grown AI talent is higher than Europe’s (60%), but trails that of the United States (89%).
59:A related statistic is that although across all levels 63,000 Chinese students studied mathematics or computer science in the United States in 2024–25, this was 20% fewer than five years previously. One reason for this drop is that the effects of the US–China geopolitical rivalry are trickling down to research, says Grace Shao, an independent analyst covering AI and technology, based in Hong Kong. A lot of Chinese people now “feel less comfortable or a feeling of animosity amongst peers”, in the United States, she says. Every Chinese student who spoke to Nature cited visa troubles as a primary concern of going to the United States. Increasingly, visas are delayed, and the US administration has sought to limit their duration, although this is being challenged in court. Because new visa rules could affect re-entry to the United States for even existing students, some US-based Chinese nationals are too anxious to visit their home country.
62:The data are not as clear on whether AI researchers already in the United States are flooding back to China. Media coverage tends to focus on high-profile returnees, such as Moonshot’s founder, Yang Zhilin, who created the Beijing-based company in 2023, having finished a PhD at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in 2019. But the true picture is more nuanced. A study by the Carnegie Endowment suggests that the United States is still able to retain high-profile AI researchers (see go.nature.com/3vxhdic ). Of its sample of authors publishing at NeurIPS, 87% of researchers of Chinese origin — those who did their undergraduate degree in China — who had been in the United States in 2019 remained there in 2025. But the Digital Science study suggests that when looking at the changing affiliations of all AI researchers actively publishing, the net direction of flow is the US losing talent to China.
65:Analyses of AI-related academic papers show China ahead of the United States in terms of sheer numbers and, increasingly, influence. The Digital Science study found that China dominates academic output — by citation as well as volume — and AI-related patents. Key universities and AI firms are spread across China, with hubs in Beijing, Shanghai, Hangzhou and Shenzhen, and with 156 research organizations each publishing more than 50 AI papers a year, the study noted. Research quality is improving, too: in 2025, for the first time, the NeurIPS conference had more lead authors based in China than in the United States or Europe, according to an analysis by The Economist (see go.nature.com/4i1ka6e ).
66:But other statistics tell a different story. Overall, the United States produces higher-impact patents and more notable AI models than China does, according to the Stanford AI Index 2026 2 . And publication data can offer a skewed portrait of AI advances, because Chinese firms are more likely to publish scientific papers than are US start-ups, according to a preprint published in July 3 . Chinese academics also report high pressure to publish papers to advance their careers.
67:Fundamentally, the United States still makes the world’s most advanced AI. Models from OpenAI and Anthropic, both based in San Francisco, California, top the leader boards for system capabilities. “China is probably somewhere between three and seven months behind the frontier in US models,” says Singer.
71:Cash is also generally less abundant in China, with private AI investment in the United States in 2025 reaching more than 23 times that invested in China, according to the Stanford report. Chinese firms’ lack of these resources is their main bottleneck, says Shao.
105:- Hook, D. DeepSeek and the New Geopolitics of AI (Digital Science, 2025).

**Authors:** Shreyasi Roy Chowdhury and Kiran Garimella

**Submitted:** 13 October 2026 (arXiv:2610.18465, cs.CY)

**Corpus:** The authors analyze a consent-based data-donation corpus of "202,590 conversations from 1,252 users" from India, Nigeria, Brazil, and Pakistan, spanning December 2022 to February 2026.

results:
ASML's third-quarter 2026 release, as shown in its SEC Form 6-K filing, reports record net sales of €11.7 billion, near the top of its guidance range. Installed Base Management sales came in at €3.3 billion and gross margin was 57.5%. The company called it a record total net sales figure, toward the high end of guidance, reflecting strong execution of its ramp-up.

The supply outlook is the notable part. CEO Christophe Fouquet said the company now expects planned supply for 2027 and 2028 to fall short of customer demand. He also said ASML is looking at ways to add capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase it had already announced. Some customers want to place orders for 2029 and 2030.

Guidance for the fourth quarter is €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion in net sales, with a gross margin of about 57%. Full-year 2026 net sales are expected at €44 billion to €45 billion, with a gross margin of about 56%.

For context, the July guidance for Q3 was €11.0 billion to €12.0 billion, and the full-year 2026 outlook was €43 billion to €45 billion. The Q3 results therefore beat the earlier Q3 range and narrowed the full-year outlook toward the top.

SCRIPT LINE: "Nature reports China has a pool of 51,000 active AI researchers compared with 14,000 in the United States, according to data from Digital Science. The same study found China dominates academic output, by citation as well as volume, and AI-related patents."
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "Nature also notes that publication data can skew the picture because Chinese firms are more likely to publish papers than US start-ups, and that Chinese academics report high pressure to publish."
PROBLEM: The script voices the dominance claim and the Digital Science conflict disclosure but drops the edition's explicit caveat that the publication data itself is skewed, leaving the output claim unqualified.

4. Block 13, Policy, regulation & law
SCRIPT LINE: "But in a parallel case, a San Francisco federal judge ruled in August that the department had violated Anthropic's First Amendment rights and that the designation was illegal retaliation."
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "a San Francisco federal judge ruled in August that the DOD had violated Anthropic's First Amendment rights and that the designation amounted to illegal retaliation."
PROBLEM: "amounted to illegal retaliation" is hardened to "was illegal retaliation".

CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "a linear classifier reads whether a request is harmful from the internal state after a single loop \"with an ROC AUC of 0.967 against 0.986 at full depth\"."
